14 15 Dstask is a personal task tracker designed to help you focus. It is similar to 16 [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) but uses git to synchronise instead of 17 a special protocol. 18 19 If you're at home in the terminal, and with solving the occasional merge 20 conflict, then dstask is for you! 21 22 https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/589d06fd-7486-46e4-b838-ce85af12f0fc 23 24 [Video courtesy of xGoivo -- thanks!](https://www.reddit.com/r/taskwarrior/comments/1o7itzg/what_do_you_guys_think_about_this_taskwarrior/) 25 26 ## Features 27 28 - Powerful context system (automatically applies filter/tags to queries and new tasks) 29 - **Git powered sync**/undo/resolve ([passwordstore.org](https://www.passwordstore.org/) style) which means no need to set up a sync server, and syncing between devices is easy! 30 - Task listing won't break with long task text 31 - `note` command -- edit a **full markdown note** for each task. **Checklists are useful here.** 32 - `open` command -- **open URLs found in specified task** (including notes) in the browser 33 - zsh/bash completion (including tags and projects in current context) for speed; PowerShell completion on Windows 34 - A single statically-linked binary 35 - import tool which can import GitHub issues or taskwarrior tasks. 36 37 ## Non-features 38 39 - Collaboration. This is a personal task tracker. Use another system for 40 projects that involve multiple people. Note that it can still be beneficial 41 to use dstask to track what you are working on in the context of a 42 multi-person project tracked elsewhere. 43 44 ## Requirements 45 46 - Git 47 - A 256-color capable terminal 48 49 ## Installation 50 51 1. Copy the executable (from the [releases page][releases]) to somewhere in your PATH. 52 - Linux/macOS: name it `dstask` and mark it executable (e.g. `/usr/local/bin/`). 53 - Windows: use `dstask.exe` and place it in a directory on `PATH` (e.g. `%USERPROFILE%\bin`). 54 1. Enable shell completions: 55 - Bash: add `source <(dstask bash-completion)` to your `.bashrc`. 56 - Zsh: add `dstask zsh-completion > /usr/local/share/zsh/site-functions/_dstask` or source completions in your `~/.zshrc`. 57 - PowerShell (Windows): see section "PowerShell completion" below. 58 1. Set up an alias in your `.bashrc`: `alias task=dstask` or `alias t=dstask` to make task management slightly faster. 59 1. Create or clone a `~/.dstask` git repository for the data, if you haven't already: 60 - Linux/macOS: `mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init` 61 - Windows: `mkdir %USERPROFILE%\.dstask && git -C %USERPROFILE%\.dstask init` 62 63 ## PowerShell completion 64 65 Save the completion script to a file and source it in your PowerShell profile: 66 67 ```powershell 68 dstask powershell-completion > ~\Documents\WindowsPowerShell\dstask-completion.ps1 69 Add-Content $PROFILE '. ~/Documents/WindowsPowerShell/dstask-completion.ps1' 70 ``` 71 72 ## Usage 73 74 Run `dstask help` for usage information. 75 76 ### Basic Commands 77 78 - `dstask add [tags] [project:name] [priority:P0-P3]` - Add a new task 79 - `dstask` or `dstask next` - Show next tasks to work on 80 - `dstask start` - Start working on a task 81 - `dstask stop` - Stop working on a task 82 - `dstask done` - Mark a task as complete 83 - `dstask edit` - Edit a task 84 - `dstask note` - Edit the markdown note for a task 85 - `dstask open` - Open URLs in task and note 86 - `dstask show-open` - Show all open tasks 87 - `dstask show-resolved` - Show completed tasks 88 - `dstask show-paused` - Show paused tasks 89 - `dstask context ` - Switch to a context (filter) 90 - `dstask sync` - Synchronise with git remote 91 92 ### Task Properties 93 94 - **Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) 95 - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` 96 - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` 97 - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` 98 - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved 99 100 ### Contexts 101 102 Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: 103 104 ```bash 105 dstask context work 106 dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work 107 dstask # shows only work tasks 108 dstask context -- # clear context 109 ``` 110 111 ### Git Sync 112 113 Sync your tasks across devices using git: 114 115 ```bash 116 # Set up sync on first device 117 cd ~/.dstask 118 git remote add origin 119 git push -u origin master 120 121 # On other devices 122 git clone ~/.dstask 123 124 # To sync 125 dstask sync 126 ``` 127 128 ### Templates 129 130 Create task templates for recurring patterns: 131 132 ```bash 133 dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 134 dstask add from-template 135 ``` 136 137 ## Best Practices 138 139 - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. 140 - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. 141 - Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context. 142 - Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately. 143 - Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this. 144 - Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top. 145 - Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up. 146 - Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks 147 - Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task 148 - Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly! 149 - set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. With direnv, this allows you to automatically switch context 150 151 ## Database 152 153 The default database location is: 154 155 - Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/` 156 - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask` 157 158 It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`. 159 160 ## Integration of fuzzy finders 161 162 Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to 163 search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell 164 wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: 165 166 ```bash 167 function dstask () { 168 local has_double_dash subcommand 169 170 if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then 171 has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" 172 subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" 173 if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ 174 [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] 175 then 176 command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ 177 | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ 178 | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ 179 | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" 180 return 181 fi 182 fi 183 184 command dstask "$@" 185 } 186 ``` 187 188 The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` 189 command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All 190 other commands are passed directly to dstask. 191 192 ## Alternatives 193 194 Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. 195 196 - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell 197 - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue 198 - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support 199 - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) 200 - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager 201 - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy 202 203 ## FAQ 204 205 > Does dstask encrypt tasks? 206 207 Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. If you want to have your remote 208 repository encrypted, you may consider 209 [git-remote-gcrypt](https://spwhitton.name/tech/code/git-remote-gcrypt/) or 210 [git-crypt](https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt). Note that dstask has not been 211 tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the 212 tools themselves. 213 214 > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? 215 216 Yes. 217 218 1. Set a context: 219 2. Run a modify command without and ID 220 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context 221 222 This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before 223 modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of 224 potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. 225 226 You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. 227 228 > Is there a GUI or web interface? 229 230 Not as part of dstask itself. However, dstask can be used as a library -- @botto 231 has started developing a web GUI, specifically to allow task management on-the-go 232 via a smartphone: . It's in early stages but 233 is meaningful as having no smartphone-based control is a blocker for a lot of people. 234 235 > Has dstask been featured in a magazine? 236 237 Yes! :-) 238 239 [releases]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases 240

**Priority**: P0 (highest), P1, P2 (default), P3 (lowest) - **Tags**: Add with `+tag`, remove with `-tag` - **Projects**: Set with `project:name` - **Due dates**: Set with `due:YYYY-MM-DD` - **Status**: open, active, paused, resolved ### Contexts Contexts automatically filter tasks and apply tags to new tasks: ```bash dstask context work dstask add finish report # automatically tagged with +work dstask # shows only work tasks dstask context -- # clear context ``` ### Git Sync Sync your tasks across devices using git: ```bash # Set up sync on first device cd ~/.dstask git remote add origin git push -u origin master # On other devices git clone ~/.dstask # To sync dstask sync ``` ### Templates Create task templates for recurring patterns: ```bash dstask add template +template project:meetings priority:P1 dstask add from-template ``` ## Best Practices - Create contexts for different areas of your life (work, home, etc.) to maintain focus. - Use tags liberally to categorize tasks, but avoid tag explosion. Use 3-5 tags per task at most. - Keep task summaries brief. Use the note field for details, checklists, and context. - Use dstask to track things you might forget, rather than everything. SNR is important. Don't track tasks for the sake of it, and don't track _ideas_. Track ideas separately. - Spend regular time reviewing tasks. You'll probably find some you've already resolved, and many you've forgotten. The `show-unorganised` command is good for this. - Try to work through tasks from the top of the list. Dstask sorts by priority then creation date -- the most important tasks are at the top. - Use `start`/`stop` to mark what you're genuinely working on right now; it makes resuming work faster. Paused tasks will be slightly highlighted, so you won't lose track of them. `show-paused` helps if they start to pile up. - Keep a [github-style check list](https://help.github.com/en/articles/about-task-lists) in the markdown note of complex or procedural tasks - Failing to get started working? Start with the smallest task - Record only required tasks. Track ideas separately, else your task list will grow unboundedly! - set `DSTASK_CONTEXT` in a `.envrc` per-project repository. With direnv, this allows you to automatically switch context ## Database The default database location is: - Linux/macOS: `~/.dstask/` - Windows: `%USERPROFILE%\.dstask` It can be configured by the environment variable `DSTASK_GIT_REPO`. ## Integration of fuzzy finders Instead of passing task IDs to commands, a fuzzy finder like [*fzf*](https://github.com/junegunn/fzf) can be used to search tasks by their summary instead. This is not part of dstask itself, but can be achieved by defining a shell wrapper like this in your `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`: ```bash function dstask () { local has_double_dash subcommand if (( $# == 1 || $# == 2 )); then has_double_dash="$( [[ "$1" == "--" || "$2" == "--" ]] && echo "1" || echo "0" )" subcommand="$( [[ "$1" == "--" ]] && echo "$2" || echo "$1" )" if (( $# == 1 || has_double_dash )) && \ [[ "${subcommand}" =~ ^(done|edit|note|open|remove|start|stop)$ ]] then command dstask show-open $( (( has_double_dash )) && echo "--" ) \ | jq -r '.[] | [.id, .summary] | @tsv' \ | fzf --delimiter='\t' --nth=2 --accept-nth=1 --preview='DSTASK_FAKE_PTY=1 dstask {1} --' \ | xargs -n1 dstask "${subcommand}" return fi fi command dstask "$@" } ``` The wrapper function checks if dstask was called with a subcommand missing the task ID, and if so uses the `show-open` command to get a list of tasks to choose from. `--` can be used to ignore the current context for the fuzzy search. All other commands are passed directly to dstask. ## Alternatives Alternatives listed must be capable of running in the terminal. - [TaskLite](https://github.com/ad-si/TaskLite) -- The CLI task manager for power users, written in Haskell - [Taskwarrior](https://taskwarrior.org/) -- the closest analogue - [Taskbook](https://github.com/klaussinani/taskbook) -- board metaphor, note support - [todo.txt-cli](https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt-cli) - [etm](https://github.com/dagraham/etm-dgraham) -- event and task manager - [t](https://github.com/sjl/t) -- a minimal todo list with an amusing philosophy ## FAQ > Does dstask encrypt tasks? Encryption is not a design goal of dstask. If you want to have your remote repository encrypted, you may consider [git-remote-gcrypt](https://spwhitton.name/tech/code/git-remote-gcrypt/) or [git-crypt](https://github.com/AGWA/git-crypt). Note that dstask has not been tested with these tools, nor can any claims be made about the security of the tools themselves. > Is it possible to modify more than one task at once with a filter? Yes. 1. Set a context: 2. Run a modify command without and ID 3. Hit y to confirm to modify all tasks in context This means it's natural to review the tasks that would be modified before modifying by listing all tasks in the current context first, instead of potentially operating blindly by matching tags or numbers. You can also specify multiple task numbers at one time, as with any other command. > Is there a GUI or web interface? Not as part of dstask itself. However, dstask can be used as a library -- @botto has started developing a web GUI, specifically to allow task management on-the-go via a smartphone: . It's in early stages but is meaningful as having no smartphone-based control is a blocker for a lot of people. > Has dstask been featured in a magazine? Yes! :-) [releases]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases

# dstask-import

usage: `dstask-import github|tw`

dstask-import is a tool to synchronize between external services or tools, and dstask.
At this point it supports importing from:

* taskwarrior
* GitHub

See below for details on each

## Taskwarrior

The import functionality is designed to aid with the transition from using taskwarrior to dstask.

Before installing dstask, you may want to export your taskwarrior database:

    task export > taskwarrior.json

After un-installing taskwarrior and installing dstask, to import the tasks to
dstask after initialising the dstask database with git:

    mkdir ~/.dstask && git -C ~/.dstask init
    dstask-import tw < taskwarrior.json

Note that the import process is lossy due to subtle differences between taskwarrior and dstask.

## GitHub

You can import issues from GitHub repositories into dstask.

### Authentication

To import from private repositories, you'll need a GitHub personal access token.
For public repositories, authentication is optional but recommended to avoid rate limits.

### Usage

To import issues from a GitHub repository:

    dstask-import github <owner>/<repo>

You can also import from multiple repositories by running the command multiple times.

## Importing data

Please see the [dstask-import tw instructions](dstask-import.md#taskwarrior) to import taskwarrior tasks.

## Using dstask

Commands and syntax are deliberately very similar to taskwarrior. Here are the exceptions:

  * The command is (nearly) always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will. If there's an ID, it can proceed the command but doesn't have to.
  * Priorities are added by the keywords `P0` `P1` `P2` `P3`. Lower number is more urgent. Default is `P2`. For example `task add eat some bananas P1`. The keyword can be anywhere after the command.
  * Action is always the first argument. Eg, `task eat some add bananas` won't work, but `task add eat some bananas` will.
  * Contexts are defined on-the-fly, and are added to all new tasks if set. Use `--` to ignore current context in any command.

[1]: https://github.com/naggie/dstask/releases/latest
